newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai plays down competition with Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai plays down competition with Hong Kong.

text.p: Shanghai is playing down its competition with Hong Kong as a major Asian financial centre, and a senior Chinese official said on Wednesday that Shanghai could anyway not replace the territory soon.

Chen Yuan, vice governor of China's central bank, said in an article published in the Beijing-based Financial News that China's economy was large enough to support financial centres in both Hong Kong and Shanghai.

"From a short term point of view, or at least until the renminbi becomes a fully freely convertible currency, it will not be possible for Shanghai to become an international finance centre," Chen said.
"Of course, given the enormous scale of China's economy, it is entirely possible that it would support the development of two financial centres," he added.

Shanghai city officials and state media are reluctant to talk about the competitive element of the relationship partly because Beijing does not want to stir fears in Hong Kong that its importance will decline after the takeover, analysts say.
The city is staging a wide range of activities to mark the approaching takeover, and the official media are pumping out Hong Kong-related features and information at a furious pace.
But there is almost nothing being said publicly on the inevitable "Tale of Two Cities" question of whether Shanghai can retrieve its mantle as premier metropolis of the China coast from Hong Kong.
"It is clear from history and industrial background that Shanghai can compete with Hong Kong to be a major financial hub in Asia," said a city official, who declined to be named.
"But we would rather work quietly and talk about this when conditions become more mature," he added.
"Competition is inevitable even though it may not be fierce at this point," said a second city official.

Before the communists arrived on its doorstep in 1949, Shanghai overshadowed every other city in East Asia. But in the decades that followed, Hong Kong powered ahead to become a major trade and finance centre.

Since the early 1990s, however, Shanghai's economic growth rate has been amongst the world's fastest, averaging 13 percent per year, and the city and its people are growing visibly more confident they will one day be back on top.
Officials have privately said they expect Shanghai to regain its top position in the regional city stakes by the middle of the 21st century.

The main problems holding Shanghai back are the city's lack of freedom to make major decisions independent of Beijing, inadequate infrastructure and the fact that the Chinese yuan is not freely convertible, analysts say.

On the other hand, Shanghai has more freedom of movement now than at any time since the communist take-over, infrastructure investment is rising fast and the markets expect the yuan to become freely convertible some time after 2000.

"We know that with its incredible development pace, strong industrial background and the central government's support, Shanghai will one day put itself in a strong competitive position with Hong Kong," an economist with the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences said.
"It is only a question of time," he said.
